title: Four Seconds Assumed, Ten Seconds Measured: MCAS, the Authorized Representatives, and the Alert That Did Not Work
participants: U.S. House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was taken was schedule and cost. The committee's first theme is "tremendous financial pressure on Boeing and the 737 MAX program to compete with Airbus' new A320neo aircraft", which "resulted in extensive efforts to cut costs, maintain the 737 MAX program schedule, and avoid slowing the 737 MAX production line" — and it identifies "several instances where the desire to meet these goals and expectations jeopardized the safety of the flying public". Keeping the aircraft inside an existing type rating is what kept the schedule and the training cost down.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was architectural and documented. MCAS was permitted "to activate on input from a single angle of attack (AOA) sensor". Boeing "failed to classify MCAS as a safety-critical system, which would have attracted greater FAA scrutiny during the certification process". And its operation "violated Boeing's own internal design guidelines", which required that the system "not have any objectionable interaction with the piloting of the airplane" and "not interfere with dive recovery". The mitigation relied on was the crew — "pilots, who were largely unaware that the system existed".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The committee calls this theme "Culture of Concealment" and gives it three documented instances: "concealing the very existence of MCAS from 737 MAX pilots"; "failing to disclose that the AOA Disagree alert was inoperable on the vast majority of the 737 MAX fleet, despite having been certified as a standard aircraft feature", while continuing "to deliver MAX aircraft to its customers knowing that" it was inoperable; and concealing "internal test data it had that revealed it took a Boeing test pilot more than 10 seconds to diagnose and respond to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator, a condition the pilot found to be 'catastrophic'". The certification case assumed four seconds. The committee: "it is inconceivable and inexcusable that Boeing withheld this information from them."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was the certification itself, obtained through a structure in which the regulated firm supplied the regulator's eyes. Boeing Authorized Representatives are "Boeing employees who are granted special permission to represent the interests of the FAA and to act on the agency's behalf in validating aircraft systems and designs' compliance with FAA requirements". The committee found "inherent conflicts of interest" in that structure, and an instance in which an AR "raised concerns internally in 2016 but did not relay these issues to the FAA" — concerns about "repetitive MCAS activation and the impact of faulty AOA data on MCAS" that "were the core contributing factors that led to the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crashes more than two years later".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment in this dossier is not a commission but an oversight relationship that had already absorbed the dissent. "Multiple career FAA officials have documented examples where FAA management overruled a determination of the FAA's own technical experts at the behest of Boeing." The committee's own verdict on the agency: "the FAA's certification review of Boeing's 737 MAX was grossly insufficient and ... the FAA failed in its duty to identify key safety problems."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Delegated certification — the long-standing arrangement under which an aircraft manufacturer's own employees are authorised to find its designs compliant on the regulator's behalf, and the grandfathering of a 1960s type certificate through successive derivative aircraft.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-MAX certification reforms and, in the committee's own framing, the case for a disclosure requirement: it notes that Boeing "was not required to share" the ten-second test result "with the FAA or Boeing customers", which is an argument about what the rules did not then demand.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The schedule pressure produced the design shortcut; the design shortcut was classified so as not to trigger the scrutiny that would have caught it; the people who would have done the scrutinising were the manufacturer's own employees; and the agency that might have overruled them had a record of overruling its own experts the other way.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the two crashes were foreign pilot error — that better-trained crews would have flown through it — or, in the other direction, that Boeing simply knew the aircraft would crash and sold it anyway.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The pilot-error account fails on Boeing's own measurements. The certification case assumed pilots would respond to the condition within four seconds; Boeing's internal simulator data showed its own test pilot taking more than ten, and that pilot called the condition "catastrophic". The crews were, in the committee's words, "largely unaware that the system existed", because its existence had been concealed from them, and the alert designed to warn of disagreeing AOA sensors was inoperable on most of the fleet while being certified as standard. The knowing-murder account fails in the other direction: what the committee documents is a chain of omissions, misclassifications and withheld data across years and many hands, not a decision to sell an aircraft expected to crash. Its five themes are about pressure, assumption, concealment, conflicted delegation and influence — and it is a committee report, which determines no liability and convicts no one.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: MCAS permitted to trigger on a single AOA sensor, not classified as safety-critical, and operating against Boeing's own internal design guidelines. Its existence concealed from the pilots expected to mitigate it. The AOA Disagree alert certified as a standard feature, found inoperable on the vast majority of the fleet, not disclosed, and aircraft delivered anyway. Internal test data showing more than ten seconds to diagnose and respond, against a four-second assumption, withheld. A Boeing Authorized Representative raising, in 2016, internally and not to the FAA, the two concerns the committee identifies as "the core contributing factors" in both crashes. FAA management overruling its own technical experts at Boeing's behest. And the committee's finding that the agency's certification review was "grossly insufficient".

citations.title: U.S. House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, Final Committee Report: The Design, Development & Certification of the Boeing 737 MAX (September 2020)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the committee's own site and read as extracted text. The report sets out "five central themes that affected the design, development, and certification of the 737 MAX and FAA's oversight of Boeing": (1) Production Pressures — "tremendous financial pressure on Boeing and the 737 MAX program to compete with Airbus' new A320neo aircraft", which "resulted in extensive efforts to cut costs, maintain the 737 MAX program schedule, and avoid slowing the 737 MAX production line", with "several instances where the desire to meet these goals and expectations jeopardized the safety of the flying public"; (2) Faulty Design and Performance Assumptions — Boeing "permitted MCAS — software designed to automatically push the airplane's nose down in certain conditions — to activate on input from a single angle of attack (AOA) sensor", "expected that pilots, who were largely unaware that the system existed, would be able to mitigate any potential malfunction", and "failed to classify MCAS as a safety-critical system, which would have attracted greater FAA scrutiny during the certification process"; the report notes MCAS's operation "violated Boeing's own internal design guidelines", which said the system should "not have any objectionable interaction with the piloting of the airplane" and "not interfere with dive recovery"; (3) Culture of Concealment — "In several critical instances, Boeing withheld crucial information from the FAA, its customers, and 737 MAX pilots. This included concealing the very existence of MCAS from 737 MAX pilots and failing to disclose that the AOA Disagree alert was inoperable on the vast majority of the 737 MAX fleet, despite having been certified as a standard aircraft feature", and Boeing "continued to deliver MAX aircraft to its customers knowing that the AOA Disagree alert was inoperable on most of these aircraft"; it also "concealed internal test data it had that revealed it took a Boeing test pilot more than 10 seconds to diagnose and respond to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator, a condition the pilot found to be 'catastrophic'", against federal guidelines that "assume pilots will respond to this condition within four seconds", and the committee adds: "While it was not required to share this information with the FAA or Boeing customers, it is inconceivable and inexcusable that Boeing withheld this information from them."; (4) Conflicted Representation — "the FAA's current oversight structure with respect to Boeing creates inherent conflicts of interest", with Boeing Authorized Representatives "granted special permission to represent the interests of the FAA and to act on the agency's behalf", and an instance in which "a Boeing AR raised concerns internally in 2016 but did not relay these issues to the FAA", concerns "about repetitive MCAS activation and the impact of faulty AOA data on MCAS" that "were the core contributing factors that led to the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crashes more than two years later"; (5) Boeing's Influence Over the FAA's Oversight Structure — "Multiple career FAA officials have documented examples where FAA management overruled a determination of the FAA's own technical experts at the behest of Boeing." The report separately finds "that the FAA's certification review of Boeing's 737 MAX was grossly insufficient and that the FAA failed in its duty to identify key safety problems." This is a congressional committee report, not a court judgment; it determines no liability and convicts no one.
